    Extras

    The Peanut Works

    Being an account of the board, the pieces, and what goes on behind them

    The board

    Every board is a honeycomb of hollows, each exactly one peanut wide. Long ago someone noticed that round things packed tight leave no room at all, and that the only way anything moves is if something else has moved first. The board has been teaching that lesson ever since.

    The golden piece

    One piece on every board was roasted a little longer than the rest, and it knows where it wants to be. It cannot get there alone. The others are not in its way out of spite; they were simply there first.

    The pieces

    A chunk is a single kernel, loose from its shell. A peanut is two, the way nature packs them. After that the shells get ambitious: threes in a row, threes in a triangle, elbows, diamonds, pods, Ys, cups and the zigzag, each with its own ideas about which way is forward. Their moves are not guesses. Every one was found by sweeping the piece through every pose it could take, and proved by following it round every circle it might touch.

    Bolts, bubbles and screws

    Bolts hold the board down where the honeycomb wore thin. Bubbles arrived with the packing crates and have been popped ever since, with great satisfaction. Turnstiles are pieces someone screwed down to keep them from wandering, which only made them better at turning.

    The classics

    Before any of this was digital it was wood: a hexagon of holes, a handful of shaped blocks, and a diamond that wanted to cross the board. Those five puzzles are here as they were, Classic Peanuts one to five.

    Behind the board

    Nobody is quite sure what is under the honeycomb. The workshop keeps the music in tune and the bolts tight, and asks only that nobody wind a piece round and round on the spot. It has never said why.

    — Slowpoke Games

    About Peanuts: A Sliding Puzzle

    Peanuts is a puzzle played on a honeycomb of circles. Each piece is one to four circles stuck together, with the little gaps between its circles filled in, so a piece can't slip through a space narrower than itself.

    How to play

    • Drag a piece. It has weight: it lags behind your pointer, bumps into its neighbours and turns when you push it against them.
    • To turn a piece in place, hold it and scroll the mouse wheel, press Q/E, or twist with a second finger.
    • Only the piece you're holding can leave the grid. Let go and it settles into the nearest holes it can reach.
    • Get the golden ★ piece onto the glowing outline. Every time a piece lands somewhere new counts as one move, however far it went.
    • Each level shows the fewest moves it can be solved in. Match it for three stars; within half again as many for two. Some levels open only once you've earned enough stars, never more than an average of 1.8 per level solved before them.
    • Stuck? The question-mark button opens your help: depending on the difficulty you chose, a glimpse of where the pieces need to get to next (G), the next move of a shortest solution (H), that move made for you (N), which pieces can move (L), and checkpoints (C to save, V to go back).
    • No mouse? Use the arrow keys (or a controller's stick) to choose a piece, Enter (or A) to pick it up, the arrows to choose where it goes and Enter again to put it there.
    • Keys: Z undo, R restart, Esc back. Settings has the full list.

    Stuck?

    Settings has a switch to open every level, whatever you've solved. Your stars and solved levels are kept.

    The levels

    Early levels in each area each need one particular way of moving their key piece: you can't finish them without it. Later levels were grown by computer search for long shortest solutions, and every move count shown was checked by an exhaustive solver.
